lead: A silicon diode needs about 0.6–0.7 V before it conducts, so a 10 mV signal through a plain diode rectifier gives no output. Putting the diode inside an op-amp feedback loop divides that drop by the loop gain, and millivolt signals rectify accurately. A capacitor after the rectifier holds the peak, and a switch plus capacitor samples the wave and holds it while an ADC converts. These circuits appear in digital multimeters, peak-reading meters, AM demodulators and ADC front ends.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.1 for the virtual short and open-loop gain, Chapter 6.2 for inverting gain, and diode behaviour from Unit 1.

blocks.text: A plain half-wave rectifier loses the first 0.6–0.7 V of every half cycle. A 10 mV peak sine therefore produces 0 V at the load; the diode never turns on. The loss is not a small error, it is the whole signal.

Place the diode in the negative-feedback path of an op-amp. The op-amp compares the output with the input and drives its own output past the diode drop until the feedback node reaches the value the closed loop demands. The diode still drops 0.6–0.7 V at the op-amp output, but the feedback node, which is the circuit output, is accurate.

blocks.where: v_D is the diode drop in volts; A_OL is the op-amp open-loop gain, a pure number; β is the feedback factor, a pure number. For the inverting rectifier β = R₁/(R₁+R_f), and for the unity-gain non-inverting follower β = 1. R₁ and R_f are the input and feedback resistors in ohms. With v_D = 0.7 V, A_OL = 10⁵ and β = 0.5 (R₁ = R_f), v_D,eff = 0.7/(10⁵ × 0.5) V = 14 µV.

blocks.text: In the inverting half-wave precision rectifier, input resistor R₁ and feedback resistor R_f set the gain when the diode conducts: v_out = −(R_f/R₁)v_in. On the other half cycle the diode is off, no current flows through R_f, and v_out = 0 V. Choose R₁ = R_f for gain −1.

A non-inverting precision rectifier applies v_in to the + input and uses a diode in the feedback path to the − input. For the half cycle that forward-biases the diode, the output follows v_in; for the other half, the diode is off and the output stays near 0 V. The op-amp may swing to a rail while the diode is off, so it must recover quickly when the next half cycle starts.

A full-wave precision rectifier uses two op-amps and two diodes. The first op-amp produces a precision half-wave signal. The second op-amp is a summing amplifier: it adds the original input and the half-wave signal with the correct signs, so the output is |v_in|. The waveform at the first op-amp output is a half-wave; the second output is the full-wave rectified sine.

These circuits work from DC to a few kHz, or tens of kHz with a fast op-amp. At higher frequency the open-loop gain falls, the loop gain available to hide the diode drop falls, and slew rate limits the output. The op-amp also takes time to come out of saturation after the diode-off half cycle.

A peak detector stores the highest input voltage on a capacitor. The non-inverting input receives v_in. A diode from the op-amp output charges hold capacitor C_H. Feedback from C_H to the inverting input keeps the diode drop inside the loop. A buffer after C_H gives a low-impedance output and stops the load from discharging the capacitor.

While v_in rises above the stored value, the op-amp drives the diode on and C_H charges. When v_in falls, the diode turns off and C_H holds the peak. A reset switch across C_H discharges it before a new measurement.

blocks.where: I_leak is the total leakage current in amperes (capacitor leakage, diode reverse leakage, op-amp bias current); C_H is the hold capacitance in farads. For I_leak = 1 nA and C_H = 0.01 µF = 10 nF, droop = 0.1 V/s = 0.1 mV/ms.

blocks.text: Peak detectors are used in peak-reading meters and AM demodulation.

A sample-and-hold, also called a track-and-hold, follows the input while the control is in track mode and freezes the last value in hold mode. An analog switch connects v_in to hold capacitor C_H. A buffer isolates C_H from the load. In track mode the buffer output follows v_in; when the switch opens, C_H holds the voltage.
An ADC needs this because its conversion takes time. If v_in changes during conversion, the digital code is uncertain. The sample-and-hold freezes the input so the ADC sees a steady voltage.

items: Acquisition time: time from switch closing until C_H settles to within a specified error of v_in.
Aperture time: delay between the hold command and the switch actually opening.
Droop rate: I_leak/C_H, the fall of the held voltage.
Hold-mode feedthrough: fraction of a changing input that couples to C_H through switch capacitance while the switch is open.

blocks.text: Applications include the digital multimeter, peak-reading meter, AM demodulator and ADC front end.

figure.caption: A 1 V sine input and the half-wave and full-wave outputs. Both rectified waves reach the full input amplitude because the diode drop is divided by the op-amp gain.

spec.aria: A sine input with the half-wave and full-wave outputs of precision rectifiers drawn from the same input, each reaching the full input amplitude.

examples.question: A 10 mV peak sine is applied to a half-wave rectifier with R₁ = R_f = 10 kΩ. (a) Find the output with a plain silicon diode. (b) Find the output with the diode inside the op-amp loop. (c) A peak detector holds 1 V on C = 0.01 µF with 1 nA leakage. Find the droop rate in V/s and mV/ms.
steps: When the diode conducts, gain = −R_f/R₁ = −10 kΩ/10 kΩ = −1.
Plain diode: the 10 mV peak is below about 0.7 V, so the diode never conducts. v_out = 0 V for both half cycles.
Precision version: the loop hides the 0.7 V. On the conducting half cycle, v_out = −1 × 10 mV = −10 mV. On the other half cycle the diode is off and v_out = 0 V.
Hold capacitance: C = 0.01 µF = 0.01 × 10⁻⁶ F = 10 nF = 10 × 10⁻⁹ F.
Droop rate = I/C = 1 nA / 10 nF = (1 × 10⁻⁹ A)/(10 × 10⁻⁹ F) = 0.1 V/s.
examples.answer: Plain diode gives 0 V; the precision rectifier gives −10 mV on one half cycle and 0 V on the other; droop is 0.1 V/s = 0.1 mV/ms.
examples.check:
peak_mV = 10.0
diode_V = 0.7
gain = -10.0 / 10.0
print(peak_mV)
print(diode_V)
print(gain * peak_mV)
print(0.0)
I = 1e-9
C = 0.01e-6
droop_V_s = I / C
print(droop_V_s)
print(droop_V_s)

traps: Using a precision rectifier above a few kHz: falling open-loop gain and slew rate distort the output, and the op-amp takes time to leave saturation.
Thinking the circuit output sits at the op-amp output: the 0.7 V diode drop appears at the op-amp output, not at the feedback node.
Confusing droop rate with ripple: droop uses I_leak/C_H and has units V/s or mV/ms; ripple belongs to power-supply filters in Unit 1.
Forgetting the reset switch in a peak detector: the capacitor keeps the old peak and the next reading is wrong.
Making the hold capacitor very small for fast acquisition: hold-mode feedthrough and charge injection then spoil the held voltage.

quiz.q: What forward voltage does a silicon diode need before it conducts strongly?
Why does placing the diode inside the op-amp feedback loop make its effective drop small?
quiz.a: The op-amp amplifies the small input error by its open-loop gain A_OL, so the diode drop is divided by the loop gain A_OL β. The feedback node, which is the output, sees only v_D/(A_OL β). For a unity-gain follower β = 1.

quiz.q: A 20 mV peak sine drives an inverting precision half-wave rectifier with R₁ = R_f = 10 kΩ. Find the output on the conducting half cycle.
quiz.a: Gain = −R_f/R₁ = −10 kΩ/10 kΩ = −1. Output = −1 × 20 mV = −20 mV.

quiz.q: Why does a full-wave precision rectifier need two op-amps and two diodes?
quiz.a: The first op-amp and its diode produce a precision half-wave signal. The second op-amp sums that half-wave with the original input with the correct signs, so both half cycles appear as positive output, giving |v_in|.

quiz.q: A peak detector uses C_H = 0.1 µF and has 10 nA of total leakage. Find the droop rate in V/s and in mV/ms.
Define acquisition time and aperture time in a sample-and-hold circuit.
quiz.a: Acquisition time is the time from closing the switch until C_H settles close to v_in. Aperture time is the delay between the hold command and the switch actually opening.

quiz.q: Why does an ADC need a sample-and-hold in front of it?
quiz.a: Conversion takes time. If the input changes during conversion, the ADC code is uncertain. The sample-and-hold freezes the input on C_H so the ADC converts a steady voltage.
It is the part of a changing input that reaches the hold capacitor through switch capacitance while the switch is open.

beyond: Not for the exam. Commercial track-and-hold ICs integrate the switch, hold capacitor and buffer, and their datasheets specify aperture jitter and feedthrough. In high-speed ADCs the sample-and-hold is usually built inside the converter. Search for track-and-hold amplifier, aperture jitter, charge injection, and precision rectifier using a current conveyor.
